Chapter 14: Distinct Until Changed

You will configure an Operator-stage comparison that suppresses repeated State candidates while allowing meaningful character changes to continue through the pipeline.

The comparator defines the product meaning of “unchanged.” The lab makes its deliberately narrow identity rule visible so you can recognize when a production comparator must also consider edits, removals, or ordering.

Suppress semantically redundant updates when repeated inputs are normal.

Applications can receive the same logical value many times: a poll may repeat its result, a selection event may reconstruct an equivalent object, or an upstream source may replay unchanged data. This chapter shows how to define “same” deliberately so redundant candidates stop early without hiding meaningful State changes.

Why this boundary matters

The service owns the comparison function and the operator evaluates the candidate before downstream filters and reducers run. The component only exposes controls and observation; it does not decide whether two values are equivalent. A comparator that is too broad can suppress a real update, so distinctness is a domain decision rather than a generic performance switch.

Use this structure for

  • repeated selection or interaction events with the same meaning
  • polling or replayed inputs that often contain unchanged State
  • expensive downstream derivation that should skip redundant work

By the end of this chapter

You will have a service-registered comparison function that accepts new character identities, suppresses equivalent candidates before downstream stages, and makes the meaning of “changed” visible in the example.

Chapter 14 Starting Point and Comparator Contract

Start with the completed Chapter 7 project. This lab updates the service, component, template, and tests. The comparator receives the incoming candidate and previous value and returns whether the candidate should be treated as unchanged. An unchanged result suppresses downstream work.

The Deliberately Narrow Rule Used Here

The displayed comparator returns unchanged when every incoming character ID already exists in the previous collection. A candidate containing a new ID continues. Object allocation and collection order do not determine the result.

Do Not Reuse This Rule for General CRUD

This identity-set rule can suppress edits to existing IDs and removal-only candidates because neither introduces a new ID. A production comparator must include every meaningful domain change—field edits, additions, removals, and ordering when order matters. A comparator that is too broad silently hides valid work.

Step 1: Configure Distinct Until Changed
↑ top

Register Distinct Until Changed with operators() in example.service.ts. The operator evaluates the resolved and merged candidate before filters and reducers, then suppresses a candidate that the comparison considers unchanged.

This is the only functional update in the example. The component and template changes provide buttons and a read-only comparison-function view so you can observe the configured behavior.

Comparator Examples
  • Same IDs and same fields: suppressed by this rule.
  • Same IDs with edited fields: also suppressed—unsafe for general CRUD.
  • Incoming subset after a removal: also suppressed.
  • At least one new ID: allowed to continue.
  • Reordered IDs only: suppressed because order is ignored.
Make the Change
  1. Install the package. 
    npm install @sdux-vault/addons
  2. Open example.service.ts then import and register withDistinctUntilChanged() through this.#vault.operators(). @for (file of serviceFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
  3. Review the identity comparison that accepts a candidate only when it introduces a new character ID.
What to Look For
  • Operators run after Resolve and Merge, before filters and reducers.
  • The first candidate proceeds; later equivalent candidates stop at the Operator stage.
  • The comparison function textarea is observational only. It does not execute from the component or template.
Suppressed-Request Contract

When the comparator returns true, the operator returns SDuX's no-op sentinel. The candidate does not reach the later Filter or Reducer stages and does not replace the committed collection. The example verifies the retained collection; it does not expose enough instrumentation to promise that every loading flag, timestamp, or other lifecycle field is unchanged. Do not build UI logic around an unobserved metadata assumption.

Reset Clears Comparison History

The registered behavior forgets its previous accepted value on reset() and destroy(). The next non-null candidate is therefore accepted as the first value, even when it is semantically equal to a value seen before reset.

Comparator Cost

This example compares small ID collections. A deep comparison of a large object graph runs for every candidate and can become expensive; prefer a stable revision, normalized identity set, or another bounded comparison when the full structure is not required.

Step 2: Update the Component and HTML
↑ top

Select Submit Same State to reconstruct Rey as a new object and merge it into the collection. The first new identity is accepted; later Rey submissions contain no new ID, so the comparison suppresses the candidate even though the object was newly allocated.

Select Submit Changed State to cycle through four distinct Jedi. Each new identity proceeds through the pipeline and updates State. After the cycle wraps, repeated identities are suppressed without relying on collection order.

Chapter Round-up
↑ top

Your example is complete when the service registers the distinct operator, repeated identities are suppressed before downstream stages, and new identities continue to update FeatureCell State. The buttons and comparison textarea make that service-owned decision visible without taking over the operator's work.

Run and Verify
  1. Select Submit Same State twice and observe that only the first accepted identity changes State.
  2. Select Submit Changed State through the four-character cycle.
  3. Inspect the Comparison Function textarea as you compare the visible collection with each request.
  4. Reset to the chapter checkpoint before repeating the sequence so the starting IDs are deterministic. Observe that a suppressed candidate does not reach the later Filter or Reducer stages.
Chapter 14 Summary
  • Distinctness is defined by the configured comparison function, not object allocation or collection position.
  • The service owns the operator registration and State updates.
  • The component and template remain presentation-only for this teaching view.
